newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay bourse chief seeks market revival measures.
newsitem.headline: Bombay bourse chief seeks market revival measures.

text.p: The head of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) on Saturday asked Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram for tax breaks to revive shaky bourses.
"It is now agreed by all concerned that our country's capital markets are in a bad shape," BSE president M.G. Damani told Chidambaram in a pre-budget memorandum.

"Individual and institutional investors have suffered heavy losses by way of capital erosion in the last eight months. Investors shall not return to the market unless the following measures are implemented immediately," Damani said.
The government is expected to present the fiscal budget for 1997/98 (April-March) in the last week of February.
Following are the main demands:
SHORT TERM MEASURES HAVING NO REVENUE IMPLICATIONS

* State-run institutions like the Life Insurance Corp (LIC), General Insurance Corp (GIC), Provident Funds, Public Provident Funds, Gratuity Funds, and Unit Trust of India (UTI) step up investments in shares and banks encouraged expertise.
* Good companies having healthy reserves be allowed to buy back their shares.
* Group companies be permitted to buy shares of listed companies in the same group and bank finance made available for this purpose.
* Banks be asked to advance against shares to investors and to stock brokers upto 70 per cent of the market value.

* Indian financial institutions and banks should not tap the Indian markets for at least the next three months since they are unable to lend at present. This would enable other needy companies to access the market.
* Companies issuing fresh capital as IPO or rights should provide safety net of one year after listing to buy back the share at issue price from subscribers up to 1,000 shares.
* Carry forward system be reviewed and transparent market friendly system introduced.
LONG TERM MEASURES HAVING REVENUE IMPLICATIONS
* Removal of minimum alternate tax.
* No tax on dividends distributed by tax paying companies.
* Long term capital gains tax payable by resident and non-resident Indians and Indian companies be brought down to 10 percent -- the same payable by foreign institutional investors.
* Tax breaks on investment in primary markets.
* Sops to lure corporate investment in mutual funds
* Exemption from payment of long-term capital gains tax in case the sale proceeds of assets sold are invested in productive assets like purchase of shares in manufacturing companies.
* Allow one time payment of long term capital gains tax to stock brokers (individuals and partnership firms), who convert themselves into corporate entities.
* Service tax on brokerage be abolished as the yield is meagre considering the effort and cost of collection.
* Stamp Act, which is a central act, be amended to do away with the multipoint taxation every time securities are traded.
"If the above measures are offered as a package, the secondary market shall become vibrant again," Damani said.
"Loss of revenue shall be insignificant considering the loss suffered by investors and the irreparable loss the nation would suffer if the sluggishness continues," he said.

Indian markets had been on the downswing for two years hit by political uncertainties and economic slowdown, but have rebounded lately in anticipation of measures to tackle sluggish industrial growth.
The 30-share benchmark BSE index ended Friday at 3,418.32 rising 154.26 points or 4.7 percent in the week -- and up nearly 11 percent since the close of 1996.
